Photograph: Rothfischer Austria Hiker reunited with backpack 60 years after he fell into a glacier in Austria Bag, camera and pipe belonging to 86-year-old are latest relics uncovered as glaciers melt due to global heating Angela Giuffrida in Rome Thu 27 Aug 2026 10.00 EDT First published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 09.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An 86-year-old mountaineer has been reunited with his backpack and climbing equipment after the kit emerged from a melting glacier in Austria – more than 60 years after he was forced to leave them there. Items including an ice axe, camera and a pipe dating from the 1950s or 1960s were discovered on the Sulztalferner glacier in Austria’s Tyrol region, at an altitude of 2,955 metres (9,700ft) above sea level, by a hiker in July. Austrian police began an investigation and through heavily frayed documents found in the backpack discovered the owner’s name and tracked him down. View image in fullscreen The belongings were discovered after glacier ice melted. Photograph: Span The man had fallen into the crevasse while crossing the glacier with friends in August 1963. The group was held together by a rope, so his friends were able to pull him free. Police said to reduce his weight he had removed his backpack and thrown it into the crevasse. They said the man, whom they did not publicly name, was too ill to collect the items himself, so they were returned to him via his son. The accelerating retreat of European glaciers, which scientists say is primarily driven by human-caused global heating, has revealed a vast array of relics, ancient ecosystems and human remains in recent decades. View image in fullscreen Frayed documents found in the bag allowed police to track down the owner. Photograph: Landespolizeidirektion Tirol In 2015, a barracks where Italian troops had sheltered while fighting the Austro-Hungarian army during the White war – a battle waged across Alpine terrain during the first world war – was discovered on Mount Scorluzzo, a peak overlooking the Stelvio pass. The bodies of dozens of soldiers, some still in their uniforms, have emerged from the melting ice in the past 20 years. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion The most extraordinary discovery of human remains on a melting glacier was made in 1991 when two German hikers found the 5,300-year-old mummified body of a hunter in the Ötztal Alps, close to Italy’s border with Austria. The body of “Ötzi the Iceman”, replete with tattoos, is on display at a museum in Bolzano. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters Australian economy Analysis The chaos in France is a ‘warning signal’ for Australia’s public spending and rising costs Patrick Commins Australia’s public debt may be well below that of France but there are lessons to be taken from its economic woes Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Mon 26 Oct 2026 10.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 10.02 EDT Share The explosion of discontent that led to major protests and violence in France and across Europe is a “warning signal” that Australia could follow the same path without an “honest conversation” about the budget, economists say. Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday to protest underfunded schools, as complaints of insufficient teacher numbers and dilapidated infrastructure mingled with broader discontent about cost-of-living pressures. Here, and across the developed world, people are struggling to cope with the affordability crisis, as households grapple with high and rising prices. The scale of the challenges in individual countries may be of a different order of magnitude, but the grievances are common. Luke Hartigan, a senior economics lecturer at the University of Sydney, said it was clear there was no single factor behind the discontent in France, but soaring energy costs were having a major impact. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Fuel prices are up 36% this year in France, or three times the increase in Australia. The US-Israel war on Iran has sent European gas prices soaring as the northern hemisphere approaches winter. Jim Chalmers faces a world of hard choices where the solution to one problem makes the other worse Read more More fundamental, however, is that France’s finances are buckling under its generous welfare state. France’s high public debt, stagnant economy, and universal social security benefits have created a “binary” situation, Hartigan said, where citizens’ demands for better services and cost-of-living help are clashing with the country’s increasingly dire fiscal position. France has not balanced its budget since 1974. Meanwhile, total public debt as a share of the economy has swelled to nearly 120%, according to the International Monetary Fund. Australia’s total government debt pile looks benign in comparison at 53%. But a decade ago our debt was 40% of GDP, and a decade before that it was just under 10%. Hartigan said France’s lacklustre economy had compounded its fiscal problems, underlining how Australia needed to work hard to boost productivity. The federal government here can still borrow and has a lot of flexibility, and the French just have no money “If you think about trajectories, they [France’s challenges] give us an idea of where we could potentially be if we continue down this path,” Hartigan said. “It’s a warning signal.” Bob Breunig, the director of the ANU’s Tax and Transfer Policy Institute, said there was a growing gap between what voters believed the government should be able to do, and what politicians were able to deliver. “One thing that is happening everywhere is this narrative that the government should be able to solve all your problems, and that narrative has probably been pushed further in Europe than it has here. It’s failing in both places, but it’s pointier there than here,” Breunig said. The evidence of this growing demand for government intervention is that French public spending now accounts for 58% of the economy, the IMF data shows. In contrast, Australia’s total public spending is equivalent to 40% of our national output – the highest in data stretching back to 1990, outside the pandemic, and at similar levels to the United States and the United Kingdom. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion “All these protesters are asking the government to help them out, but the government has maxxed out the credit card,” Breunig said, who said France’s debt was “reaching levels that are unmanageable”. 1:44 Police and protesters exchange teargas and fireworks in demonstrations across France – video “The federal government here can still borrow and has a lot of flexibility, and the French just have no money.” President Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power has been marked with failed attempts to rein in spending. “There’s a real sense that people don’t know what to do,” Breunig said. The bond market reflects growing alarm with France’s fiscal trajectory. France typically has to pay a higher interest rate on its 10-year debt than fiscally prudent Germany, and the gap between the two rates is a measure of financial markets’ confidence in France’s fiscal position. That gap is now at its widest since the European debt crisis in 2011. Amid structural pressures on the budget from an ageing population, the NDIS, higher interest rates, and the push for greater spending on national defence, Breunig agreed there were lessons for Australia in not allowing the country to drift too far and for too long. “We need an honest public conversation about what the government can be expected to do and what it can’t, and then a conversation about how much that would cost and whether we are willing to pay for that.” While the opposition has attacked what it sees as the deadening effect of high government spending on economic dynamism, Breunig said he was broadly “agnostic” whether repairing the budget involved lower spending or higher taxes. “At the end of the day, making these decisions is exactly what democracy is for.” Explore more on these topics Australian economy Australian politics France analysis Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Australia World AU politics Environment Climate crisis Indigenous Australia Immigration Media Business Health Science Tech Podcasts Newsletters
